questions.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.explain: Git records history locally and works without any website. GitHub (like GitLab or Bitbucket) hosts copies of repositories so a team can share them.
options: They are the same program with two names
Git is the version control system on your computer; GitHub is a website that stores Git projects online for sharing
GitHub runs on your computer; Git is the website
Git only works when you are connected to GitHub

questions.q: Why does the lesson run git config --global user.name and user.email first?
questions.explain: Git stamps each commit with who made it. --global saves the setting for every project on this computer.
options: Every commit you record carries this name and e-mail
To set the password for pushing

questions.q: What does git init do?
questions.explain: After git init nothing is recorded yet: git status shows your files as untracked until you add and commit them.
options: Turns the current folder into a repository by creating a hidden .git folder, where the history lives
Commits every file in the folder

questions.q: git status lists server.js under Untracked files. What does that mean?
questions.explain: An untracked file becomes part of the history only after git add and git commit. Ignored files are not listed as untracked at all.
options: The file has a syntax error
Git sees the file but is not recording it yet

questions.q: What are the two steps to record a change?
questions.explain: The staging area is the list of what goes into the next commit. This lets you choose exactly which changes a commit contains.
options: git add puts files on the staging area; git commit takes the snapshot with a message

questions.q: Which is the best commit message?
questions.explain: A good message says what the commit does, in a few words. "stuff" and "fix" tell a reader nothing when they look back through the history.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say to commit small and often?
questions.explain: One commit per finished step means each commit has one clear purpose, and a bad change can be found and undone without touching the rest.
options: GitHub charges less for small commits
A history of small commits is easy to read, and easy to undo one piece at a time
Git cannot store commits with more than one file
Small commits run the tests automatically

questions.q: Why does node_modules/ not belong in the repository?
questions.explain: Commit the two package files instead. Anyone who clones the repository runs npm install and gets the exact same packages.
options: It is thousands of files that npm install recreates from package.json and package-lock.json at any time
npm deletes it after every install

questions.q: Why must .env never go into a repository?
questions.explain: A repository is copied to every developer, to GitHub and often to CI servers. Secrets stay in .env on your own computer, listed in .gitignore.
options: Because Git cannot read files that start with a dot
It holds secrets such as the database password, and anyone who can read the repository could read them
Because Node.js deletes it on start

questions.q: When should you create .gitignore with node_modules/ and .env?
questions.explain: One careless git add . records everything Git is offering to track. With .gitignore in place first, those files never reach a commit.
options: After the first push, when GitHub warns you
Before your first git add ., so they are never recorded
Only when the repository becomes public
Never; delete the files before each commit instead

questions.q: Should the .gitignore file itself be committed?
questions.explain: .gitignore is ordinary project configuration. Committing it protects every teammate from adding .env or node_modules/ by accident.
options: No, it is private to each developer
Yes, so everyone on the team gets the same rules
No, Git reads it from GitHub

questions.q: A file does not show up in git status and you wonder why. Which command tells you which line of .gitignore hides it?
questions.explain: git check-ignore -v prints the .gitignore file, the line number and the pattern that matched, for example .gitignore:2:.env.

questions.q: What is a .env.example file for?
questions.explain: The example file documents what the app needs without leaking anything. The real values live only in each developer's own .env.
options: A backup of the real .env, with all its values
It lists the variable names with no real values, so a new developer knows what to fill in; it is committed
It is loaded by Node.js instead of .env in production
It is a file Git creates when .env is ignored

questions.q: Which of these should you commit in a Node.js project?
questions.explain: package-lock.json lets anyone reinstall the exact same package versions. node_modules/ is generated, .env is secret, and log files are local.

questions.q: What does git switch -c port-from-env do?
questions.explain: Without -c, git switch main moves to an existing branch. With -c it creates a new one first.
options: Creates the branch port-from-env and moves to it
Commits all changes with the message port-from-env

questions.q: You changed server.js (already tracked) and created a new file health.js. What does git commit -am "Update" record?
questions.explain: -a stages every tracked file that changed. Git does not know health.js yet, so it stays untracked.
options: Only server.js; the new file needs git add first

questions.q: When does git merge stop with a merge conflict?
questions.explain: Changes to different lines merge by themselves. A conflict is normal, not an error: Git asks you to decide.
options: Whenever both branches have new commits
When both branches changed the same lines, so Git cannot know which version you want
When one branch added a new file
When the branch name contains a dash

questions.q: You have a merge conflict in server.js. What are the steps to finish the merge?
questions.explain: git add marks the file as resolved. If the merge gets confusing, git merge --abort puts everything back as it was before the merge.
options: Run git merge again until it works
Edit the file to hold the final code, delete all three marker lines, git add server.js, then commit

questions.q: After merging port-from-env you run git branch -d port-from-env. What happens to its commits?
questions.explain: A branch is just a name that points at a commit. After the merge, main contains those commits, so the name is no longer needed.
options: They are deleted from the history
They stay in the history; only the branch name is removed
They move to a hidden branch called deleted

questions.q: You merge a branch into main, and main got no new commits in the meantime. What happens?
questions.explain: Nothing needs combining, so main simply moves to the branch's last commit and the graph stays a straight line.
options: A fast-forward: Git just moves main forward, with no merge commit
Git creates a merge commit with three parents

questions.q: You committed .env by mistake, and have not pushed yet. What does the lesson do?
questions.explain: Nothing left your computer, so undoing the commit is enough. A new commit on top would still leave the secret in the history.
options: Push it and delete it on GitHub
git reset HEAD~1: move the branch back one commit and keep the files, so .env is an ignored file again

questions.q: A database password was pushed to GitHub. What must you do first?
questions.explain: Treat it as stolen: bots scan pushes within minutes, and others may already have pulled a copy. Only a new secret really protects you; cleaning the history comes after.
options: Rewrite history with git filter-repo and force-push
Rotate the secret: change the password, revoke the key, create a new one

questions.q: What does git rm --cached .env do?
questions.explain: --cached means "only in Git". Add .env to .gitignore too, and remember the old value is still in the history.
options: Deletes .env from your disk and from Git
Stops tracking .env but keeps the file on your disk

questions.q: What does GitHub push protection do?
questions.explain: Secret scanning finds known secret formats in pushed code and alerts you; push protection goes further and stops the push. Neither replaces rotating a secret that leaked.
options: Blocks pushes from people without a paid plan
Blocks a push that contains a recognised secret before it is published

questions.q: What does -u do in git push -u origin main?
questions.explain: origin is the usual name of your main remote. After the first -u push, git push and git pull know where to go.
options: Remembers the link between your main and origin/main, so later a plain git push is enough

questions.q: Git asks you to log in the first time you push to GitHub. What does GitHub accept?
questions.explain: GitHub does not accept your account password for Git. Tokens and SSH keys can be limited and revoked on their own, without changing your password.
options: Your GitHub account password typed into the terminal
A browser login through Git Credential Manager, a personal access token, or an SSH key
No login at all for private repositories

questions.q: You git clone the Task API onto a new computer. What else do you need before it runs?
questions.explain: The clone has the full history but, correctly, no generated packages and no secrets. .env.example shows which variables to fill in.
options: Run npm install and create your own .env, because neither node_modules nor .env is in the repository

questions.q: What is a pull request?
questions.explain: Teams do not push straight to main. Teammates read the diff, automated tests run, and the branch is merged only when it is approved and the checks pass.
options: A command that downloads commits from GitHub
GitHub's way to propose a branch, have it reviewed and checked, and then merge it
A request to GitHub support for help
A way to push straight to main faster

questions.q: This is the lesson's toy secret scanner, with one pattern. What does it print?
questions.explain: Only the first line has user:password@ after //. The code that reads process.env contains no secret at all, which is the pattern to follow.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pattern needs AKIA followed by exactly 16 capital letters or digits. AKIA123 is too short, and the regex is case-sensitive, so the lower-case line does not match.

questions.q: This is the pattern from the "Extend the scanner" exercise. What does it print?
questions.explain: The value must be 16 or more non-space characters. An empty value (as in .env.example) and a short value are not flagged; PORT has no secret-like name.
options:
API_KEY=0123456789abcdef0123 true
API_KEY= false
DB_PASSWORD=short false
PORT=3000 false

API_KEY=0123456789abcdef0123 true
API_KEY= true
DB_PASSWORD=short true
PORT=3000 false

API_KEY=0123456789abcdef0123 true
API_KEY= false
DB_PASSWORD=short true
PORT=3000 false

questions.q: This is the lesson's required helper, reading from a plain object instead of process.env. What does it print?
questions.explain: An empty string is falsy, so an empty DATABASE_URL counts as missing. Failing at startup with a clear message beats a confusing database error later.
options:
Missing environment variable PORT.
Missing environment variable DATABASE_URL.

questions.q: The lesson logs only the host of the database URL. What does this print?
questions.explain: host is only the host name and port. The whole URL contains the password, so it must never be logged.
questions.code:
const databaseUrl = "https://app:s3cret@db.example.com:5434/taskdb";
console.log("Connecting to", new URL(databaseUrl).host);

questions.q: A script reads git status --short --ignored. What does it print?
questions.explain: In short status, A means "added to the staging area" and !! marks ignored files. slice(3) drops the two-letter code and the space.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: From <<<<<<< HEAD to ======= is the version on your current branch (main, with the log message). After ======= comes the branch you are merging.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: git log --oneline prints the short hash, one space, and the message. commits[1] is the second line.
options: { hash: '9a2086f', message: 'Log when the server starts' }
{ hash: '9a2086f', message: ' Log when the server starts' }
{ hash: '9a2086f Log', message: 'when the server starts' }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In git diff, lines starting with - were removed and lines starting with + were added. Changing one line shows as one removal and one addition.

questions.q: Write a tiny .gitignore matcher. isIgnored(path, patterns) returns true when any pattern matches. Three kinds of pattern: one ending in / is a folder (matches paths inside it, e.g. node_modules/ matches node_modules/pg/index.js); one starting with * matches paths ending with the rest (*.log); anything else matches the file name exactly (the part after the last /).
questions.explain: Notice that .env.example is not ignored: it holds names only and should be committed. The real Git rules have more cases, but these three cover a typical Node.js project.
questions.expected:
node_modules/pg/index.js true
.env true
config/.env true
logs/app.log true
.env.example false
server.js false

questions.q: Finish checkMessage(message). It returns a list of problems: "empty" if the trimmed message is empty (return only that one); "too vague" if the whole lower-cased message is one of stuff, fix, wip, changes; "too long" if it is longer than 50 characters; "start with a capital" if the first character is a lower-case letter.
questions.explain: A good message says what the commit does, in a few words, like "Read the port from PORT". Teams often run a check like this automatically before a commit is accepted.
questions.expected:
[]
[ 'too vague', 'start with a capital' ]
[ 'empty' ]
[ 'too long', 'start with a capital' ]

questions.q: Before committing a resolved conflict, make sure no marker is left. Finish markerLines(text): return the line numbers (starting at 1) of lines that start with <<<<<<<, ======= or >>>>>>>.
questions.explain: Resolving a conflict means deleting all three marker lines. A marker left in a .js file is a syntax error that breaks the server.

questions.q: Finish scan(fileName, text) like the lesson's scanner: for each line that matches any pattern, add "file:line looks like a NAME" (line numbers start at 1).
questions.explain: Real scanners (GitHub secret scanning, push protection) work the same way with hundreds of patterns. Code that reads process.env has nothing to find.
questions.expected:
[
  '.env:2 looks like a GitHub token',
  '.env:3 looks like a URL with a password'
]
[]

questions.q: Turn a .env text into a safe .env.example: finish toExample(text) so every line NAME=value becomes NAME=. Keep empty lines and lines starting with # as they are.
questions.explain: .env.example is committed, so it must hold names only. The real values stay in your own .env, which .gitignore keeps out of the repository.

questions.q: Finish branchName(title) to turn a task title into a branch name like done-filter: lower case, every run of characters that are not a-z or 0-9 becomes one -, and no - at the start or end.
questions.explain: Short, lower-case branch names with dashes, like port-from-env, are easy to type in git switch and git push -u origin.
